articles.title: The Limit of Nature: Thucydides and the Politics of Theory
articles.abstract: This article reconsiders Thucydides’s role as a foundational theorist of human nature. Contrary to conventional readings, I argue that Thucydides approaches “nature” ( physis ) less as a universal principle of behavior than as a site of political and theoretical investigation. By distinguishing his authorial voice from those of his speakers, I demonstrate that his analysis consistently approaches human nature as a limit concept—a baseline and boundary of human capacity that emerges in moments of existential precarity—while introducing a more nuanced set of terms to describe the habitual behaviors of political groups. By nevertheless foregrounding the more robust and determinative concept of nature in moments of contentious deliberation, Thucydides encourages reflection on the political dynamics that generate essentialist theories in public discourse. His account thus serves as a helpful point of reference for thinking about how competitive, polarizing speech affects the substantive categories of political debate and analysis, and through them political action.

articles.title: How Sociotropic Aesthetic Judgments Drive Opposition to Dense Housing Development
articles.authors: DAVID E. BROOCKMAN, CHRISTOPHER S. ELMENDORF, JOSHUA L. KALLA
articles.abstract: Voter opposition to dense housing development contributes to America’s housing shortage. Prevailing explanations emphasize homeowner self-interest and “NIMBYism.” We develop a theory of how sociotropic aesthetic judgments shape housing policy preferences and demonstrate its unique implications with a series of descriptive studies and experiments. First, people who choose to live in dense neighborhoods have an aesthetic taste for density, leading homeowners in already-dense areas to be more supportive of dense development both in their neighborhoods and elsewhere. Second, voters are more supportive of dense development when it is proposed in already-dense neighborhoods where it “fits”—even voters who live in those same dense neighborhoods. Finally, genuine aesthetic distaste for tall buildings is widespread and causally affects support for development. Our findings offer a new lens for understanding housing policy preferences and suggest novel solutions for addressing America’s housing shortage.

Environmental clash? The environmental dimension and electoral preferences in six European democracies
articles.authors: Silvia Bolgherini, Luca Carrieri, Matteo Giardiello
articles.abstract: The political debate over environmental issues in Europe has grown increasingly contested and likely influences voting behaviour. Yet most research treats environmental voting as a single environmental protection versus economic growth dichotomy. This article reconceptualises the “environmental issue” as a composite “environmental dimension” integrating socio-economic trade-offs concerning household consumption, public services, economic growth, and employment. We rely on original survey data from six EU member states (France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain and Sweden), testing the association between this composite dimension and the vote intentions for European party families. By performing logistic regression models separately for each party family, our findings yield two main results. First, anti-environmental attitudes are systematically correlated with the electoral preferences of Radical Right parties. Second, pro-environmental orientations are associated with voting intentions for Greens, Social-Democrats, Radical Left, and also Christian Democratic/Conservative parties. In brief, the environmental dimension generates widespread and two-sided electoral responses among supporters of different party families, constituting a significant correlate of their voting preferences.

Can you feel the group appeal tonight?: MPs’ conveyed emotions in disability representation in Western Europe
articles.abstract: Parties use group appeals to connect or distance themselves from certain social groups. Existing research focuses mostly on well-established groups, like social class, often neglecting marginalized groups, such as persons with disabilities. This study investigates disability group appeals and their symbolic dimension in parliamentary speeches from 1997 to 2019 across Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, and Ireland, employing transformer-based models to identify group appeals and analyze emotional context. Findings reveal country and party ideology differences in group appeal usage and a gender effect, indicating women are more likely to appeal to persons with disabilities. This research offers a methodological framework applicable to other marginalized groups and proposes adding a substantive dimension to the study of group appeals.

articles.title: The devil is in the divisor: Deviations from proportionality in Dutch municipal coalition negotiations, 1998 – 2022
articles.abstract: Under what circumstances do parties get a share of executive posts that is not directly proportional to their legislative seats? While there is strong empirical support for Gamson’s law, i.e., the distribution of executive posts in a coalition is directly proportional to the negotiating parties’ number of legislative seats, we know little about when deviations from this pattern occur. To get a grip on these deviations, we study coalition negotiations at the Dutch local level between 1998 and 2022. Major deviations from Gamson’s law are rare, and most deviations occur because no strictly proportional solution was available. Small parties are usually overrepresented and large parties are usually underrepresented. The norm of proportionality is very strong: divisor methods that distribute executive posts over parties according to their legislative seats help predict how these posts are distributed. There is no consistent evidence that parties’ bargaining power affects the direction or size of divergences.

Ideological (a‐)symmetries in moral judgments of online hate
articles.authors: Vladimir Bojarskich, Meltem Yucel, Lindsay Hahn, Tobias Rothmund
articles.abstract: Political ideology is key in how we react to social and political events, but how does it predict moral judgments of online hate? The contextual symmetry hypothesis suggests that conservatives and liberals condemn online hate similarly when it targets ideologically favored groups. The generalizable asymmetry hypothesis proposes that conservatives, compared to liberals, are less condemning of hate comments regardless of the target. Across experiments in Germany ( N = 903) and the United States ( N = 490), we found consistent evidence for the contextual symmetry account: Conservatives and liberals differ in their sensitivity toward online hate depending on the target and ground their moral judgments on perceptions of the aggressor's responsibility and the victim's vulnerability and suffering. These findings suggest that public divisions over hate speech regulation may reflect ideological differences in perceptions of victim vulnerability, suffering, and perpetrator responsibility, rather than a general conservative tendency to condone online hate.

articles.title: A sentiment-based approach to measuring multidimensional party positions using transformer
articles.abstract: Existing automated position scaling models from texts rely on the conflict-driven assumption, forcing models to search the linguistic space for differentiating features between political subjects. This leads models to conflate rhetorical styles with political sentiments when subjects are not inherently conflictual. This article introduces ContextScale, a sentiment-based position scaling framework leveraging pre-trained Transformer models to predict policy topics and political sentiments and measure topic-specific position scores across multiple policy dimensions at the sequence level. ContextScale offers an alternative way to gauge party positions, focusing on how political texts express attitudes toward policy issues rather than on contrast between actors. Validity tests demonstrate its ability to capture nuances in party positioning and its adaptability across languages, text domains, and theoretical models.

articles.title: City representation in Washington: determinants and responses
articles.abstract: When and why do cities lobby the federal government? Although intergovernmental lobbying has grown, variation in municipal lobbying remains insufficiently understood. We link city lobbying to congressional representation, arguing that poorly aligned cities hire lobbyists to compensate for representational shortfalls and that municipal competition can encourage lobbying when other local governments press competing claims. Using city-level data from 2008 to 2018, we find strong support for the alignment expectation and evidence that competition matters conditionally on a city’s position within the district, but little evidence that competition moderates the effect of city–members of Congress alignment. The results recast intergovernmental lobbying as both a substitute for weak ex ante representation and a strategy through which cities seek influence in shared congressional constituencies.

articles.title: Sustaining democracy under the shadow of force
articles.authors: Zhaotian Luo, Adam Przeworski, Hongding Zhu
articles.abstract: Democracy faces two threats: incumbents may peacefully monopolize office, or political factions may seek power through violent conflict. Using a dynamic model, the authors examine some conditions under which democracy is sustainable against both threats. Two parties vie for office under the shadow of force. To resolve conflict, the incumbent can share revenue as well as hold competitive elections: each time, it chooses the probability of losing the next election and redistributes revenue. Elections enable the incumbent to concede control over revenue over time but come with regular risks of defeat. Democracy is sustainable if the economic stakes in elections are neither too low nor too high, while the military strength is sufficiently balanced between the two parties. When the stakes are high, democracy may be sustained only with civilian control of the military or programmatic transfers.
